important_facts_missed: Godot 4.8 is in beta (beta 1 about 15 Oct 2026, beta 3 around now), with stable expected late 2026. Plan for an upgrade mid-project. I found no web/WebGPU change in it.

Safari 26 (Sept 2025; macOS Tahoe 26, iOS/iPadOS 26) ships WebGPU on by default, and Chrome has WebGPU too. Godot cannot use it officially. PlayCanvas, Babylon and Three.js can, and that changes the Safari/iPad picture in their favour.

An unofficial Godot WebGPU fork exists (dwalter/godotwebgpu, based on 4.6.2, beta), and there was a GodotCon Boston 2026 talk on it. It is not production-ready, but it is the only WebGPU route for Godot.

Official PlayCanvas Editor MCP server (about 125 tools, MIT, Node 22.18+). This partly closes the 'editor is GUI-only' gap, though it needs an open, connected browser Editor tab, which conflicts with a creator who prefers not to have the agent drive the browser.
The PlayCanvas PhysicsWorld backend layer is documented. Jolt, Rapier and PhysX are listed as candidate engines, and a community Jolt components package exists.

Babylon.js ships an official Havok physics plugin (wasm). This is from prior knowledge and was not re-verified this session. That makes Babylon's built-in physics arguably stronger than PlayCanvas's ammo.js. The report left Babylon physics unresearched.
Godot Compatibility per-mesh light limits (8 omni + 8 spot by default). These matter for a neon street full of lights.
Lightmaps can only be baked on RenderingDevice hardware (the Mac's Forward+), then rendered in Compatibility, so the build pipeline must bake natively before the web export.
Godot headless web export needs the matching 4.7.2 export templates downloaded and installed first. This is a CLI-doable step the report did not mention.

Headless Chromium in Playwright often falls back to software WebGL (SwiftShader), so automated browser screenshots and FPS numbers may not reflect real GPU performance. Headed or GPU-enabled runs are needed for meaningful perf tests of any of these engines.
Godot loading-test sizes have no stated hardware or network and no load-time numbers. No 4.7 row exists.
verification.bias_check: The report is mostly accurate on Godot's documented web limits. It slightly oversold Godot on agent-workflow and continuity grounds. It claimed an existing project for this game, which the context does not support, and it leaned on small community MCP servers whose web-build coverage is nil. It undersold the web-native options: it missed Safari 26's default WebGPU, the official PlayCanvas Editor MCP server, the PlayCanvas physics backend layer, and Babylon's Havok physics. Its version and date facts hold up apart from the missed Godot 4.8 beta. Its reasoning that assets, not the engine runtime, dominate download size is sound but rests on unmeasured assumptions.
verification.corrected_bottom_line: Godot 4.7.2 Web is a viable vertical-slice path. It has built-in character and vehicle nodes, text scenes, and a headless CLI export that an agent can drive. But it is locked to WebGL2/Compatibility with no official WebGPU even in the 4.8 beta. That means faked wet-neon effects, per-mesh light caps, limited web audio, and Safari WebGL2 caveats, and its agent test tools exercise the native build, not the browser build. The web-native engines are stronger on browser tech than the report credited: Safari 26 and Chrome both ship WebGPU, PlayCanvas has an official Editor MCP server, and Babylon has Havok physics. The cost is that the agent writes more glue code, and authoring in an editor still needs a live browser tab. Godot is not the obvious winner by default, because no project exists for this game yet. A short spike that measures one rainy neon street with real assets in Godot Web vs Babylon or PlayCanvas, on Chrome and Safari, is the honest way to decide. Unity is not installed and was not assessed here.

research.summary: Evidence on precedents is thinner than the hype suggests. I found no shipped, polished first-person driving city game in a browser from 2023-2026 with published size, performance and post-mortem data. The nearest open precedents are an open-source Vilnius driving prototype (Three.js, built with Claude, October 2026, 'early playable prototype', 60 fps on an M-series laptop, no traffic, pedestrians, police or audio yet) and EverRealm, a first-person open-world RPG on Three.js with about 1,800 NPCs (September to October 2026). Both are small, solo and unproven at scale, and neither gives a download size. Documented AI-agent-built 3D browser games are mostly demos and prototypes made in days; the only stated failure modes I could verify are performance and memory hygiene (draw calls, no dispose(), oversized models, pixel ratio, post-processing). Performance budgets are consistent across sources: draw calls are the binding constraint, not triangles. Desktop tolerates hundreds of draw calls and mobile about 100. A rainy neon night city with traffic and pedestrians is feasible on an M4 only with instancing, baked or fake lighting, a handful of real lights, and an adaptive quality governor. WebGPU is now shipped in Chrome/Edge (113+), Safari 26+ (macOS/iOS), and Firefox on Windows (141) and Apple Silicon Mac (145 on macOS 26+, 147 on all macOS), with Firefox Android and Linux still partial. Three.js WebGPURenderer falls back to WebGL 2 automatically. Unity web has a hard 2GB heap and iOS Safari crash reports, and Godot 4.7.2's web export wasm is about 39.5 MB raw (about 10 MB gzipped) before any game content. Several sources are blogs, forum posts or video pages, not primary docs. Firecrawl credits ran out mid-run, so some planned pages (Reddit 4-games thread, Unity 50MB thread, Reddit WebGPU benchmark) were not opened.

claims.topic: precedent: open-world driving city in browser
claims.claim: An open-source browser open-world game of real Vilnius (Three.js, 1:1 scale) is playable with walking, driving and a tyre-physics car, reported at 60 fps on an Apple M-series laptop. It streams the city's photogrammetry mesh with LOD, a GPU memory budget, a frame-time quality governor and dynamic resolution. Traffic, pedestrians, police, audio and saving are listed as not started, and it is labelled an early playable prototype. It was co-authored by Claude Opus 5.5 (commit Oct 18, 2026). Download size is not stated: the city mesh streams from a municipal server and the repo asks for about 3 GB of disk for data.
claims.evidence: README: 'What works today' table; 'Quests, NPCs, police, audio, saving: Not started'; commit co-author line; 'No releases published'; 1 star.

claims.topic: precedent: AI-built game stack and testing
claims.claim: The Vilnius project was built with an AI agent. It uses Node/Vite with plain Three.js JS modules, Python for the data pipeline and headless Blender for tile building. Its agent-friendly test is a headless Chromium script (Playwright) that plays the game with key presses and checks physics, memory, frame times and console errors. It also carries an uncompiled Unreal project ('written but never compiled'), which is evidence of agent-written code that was never verified.
claims.evidence: README 'Testing' paragraph and the Unreal row ('written but never compiled'); languages JS 60%, Python 28.5%, C++ 9.8%.

claims.topic: precedent: first-person open world on Three.js with crowds
claims.claim: EverRealm is a first-person open-world RPG in the browser (Three.js, Vite, cannon-es physics) with chunked terrain streaming, a city of nearly 1,700 buildings and about 1,800 citizens. It uses one InstancedMesh per building model, billboard crowds on a shared InstancedMesh, and full skinned NPCs only within about 40 units (swapped back past 65). Quality is a ladder of discrete tiers (Low to Ultra) driven by a frame-rate governor that only steps down (30 fps floor, 6 s median windows, 10 s warm-up). It runs on itch.io. No download size was given and the post is a self-reported solo showcase.
claims.evidence: Forum showcase post and replies (Sep 21 to Oct 5, 2026) describing instancing, billboard LOD and the one-way governor.

claims.claim: Where vibe-coded Three.js scenes break: oversized models (tens of MB GLBs, 4096px textures cause long loads and mobile tab reloads), missing dispose() leaks (geometries/textures counters keep climbing and fps drops after scene changes), too many draw calls (no instancing or merging), unbounded devicePixelRatio, and post-processing passes (bloom/SSAO can halve fps on phones). It notes AI-generated scenes rarely instance or dispose, so a dedicated optimisation pass is needed. This is a commercial resource site, not a measured study, and says nothing about collision or physics bugs.
claims.evidence: Fetched page lists 'five most common causes'; the search snippet adds that AI-generated scenes rarely instance or dispose.

claims.claim: Public accounts of AI-agent-built Three.js games are mostly short-timeline projects (for example a game built in about two days with Claude Code, and a 'zero code' 3D game generator tutorial). One reported tip is to build an in-game configurator with sliders to cut back-and-forth with the agent. I did not find a verified post-mortem of an AI-built game at the scale of an open driving city with traffic, AI and mission systems beyond the Vilnius prototype.
claims.evidence: daily.dev summary of a May video (Laser Nuke, two days, Claude Code) and Meshy tutorial pages. Only search snippets were read, not the originals.

claims.claim: The widely quoted guidance from a Three.js maintainer is roughly under 100 draw calls and under 100,000 vertices for mobile. A 2026 blog says desktop machines handle several hundred to low thousands because the real cost is CPU-side submission. Another blog's rule of thumb for smooth 60 fps on mid-range hardware is about 100-150 draw calls and a couple of million triangles. Triangle count matters less than draw calls, and instancing and batching (InstancedMesh, BatchedMesh) are the main levers. These are rules of thumb from blogs, not benchmarks on specific chips.
claims.evidence: Item 30 cites the three.js forum quote; the second post gives its own budget; it warns that an M-series Mac hides problems.

claims.claim: WebGPU is not automatically faster. A 2026 Three.js blog says WebGPU helps most with many draw calls and compute, and forum users report scenes where WebGPURenderer is slower than WebGLRenderer. A Reddit test snippet reports draw calls dropping from 331 to 171 in one scene, but 'not automatically faster on every device'. I could not open the Reddit post, so treat that as unverified.
claims.evidence: utsubo 'Three.js in 2026' page text and the Reddit search snippet.

claims.claim: WebGPU shipped in Chrome/Edge 113 on Mac, Windows and ChromeOS. It reached Android in Chrome 121 (Android 12+, ARM/Qualcomm/Intel GPUs) and Linux Intel Gen12+ in Chrome 144. Caniuse shows Chrome versions up to 160 as supported, and Android Chrome 157 as supported. Global support is shown as about 88.6%, with Safari desktop marked 'partial'.
claims.evidence: gpuweb Implementation Status wiki and caniuse (fetched Nov 2026).

claims.claim: Safari 26 on macOS Tahoe 26, iOS 26, iPadOS 26 and visionOS 26 ships WebGPU enabled by default. Caniuse lists iOS Safari 26.0-27.2 as supported, but desktop Safari 26-27.x as 'partial', meaning enabled by default only on macOS 26 Tahoe or later. Firefox shipped it on Windows in 141 (July 2025), Apple Silicon Mac on macOS 26+ in 145 and all macOS versions in 147. Linux and Android are still Nightly or behind a flag, and Mozilla expected to do Android work in 2026. Caniuse's 'Firefox: disabled by default' row conflicts with the wiki's shipping versions; the wiki is the more detailed source.
claims.evidence: gpuweb wiki Safari and Firefox tables; web.dev announcement of Nov 25, 2025; caniuse notes.

claims.claim: Three.js WebGPURenderer falls back to a WebGL 2 backend automatically (or via forceWebGL), so one codebase can cover browsers without WebGPU. The release history lists r184 on April 16, 2026 and r187 as the latest at the time of that article. r184 added TSL materials on WebGLRenderer and FSR 1 / TAAU upscaling nodes. Version churn is a risk: r186 removed PCFSoftShadowMap and minified builds.
claims.evidence: utsubo 2026 changelog page and the official WebGPURenderer docs showing the forceWebGL option.

claims.claim: Unity 6's web heap can grow only up to 2 GB, and automatic resizing can crash if the browser cannot find a contiguous address block. The manual says mobile browsers need advanced tuning and does not cover iOS Safari. A forum thread reports that Unity 6 advertised 4 GB support but a game still crashed on iOS even with 4 GB devices. A separate thread title claims a 50 MB build limit for phones, which I could not open.
claims.evidence: Unity 6000.1 manual 'Memory in Unity Web' (fetched); forum excerpts (Nov 2024).

claims.topic: Godot web export size and constraints
claims.claim: A Godot 4.7.2 single-threaded web export has an index.wasm of 39,514,754 bytes (about 10.1 MB gzip -9) before any game content. Thread support needs Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy headers (SharedArrayBuffer). Cloudflare Pages caps files at 25 MiB, below the raw wasm size. Godot 4 C# projects cannot export to the web. The source is a vendor blog (Ziva), but it reports its own test.
claims.evidence: Table of file sizes and FAQ in the blog; dated Nov 5, 2026 for hosting limits.

research.performance_notes:
What the evidence supports for a rainy neon night city on integrated GPU or Apple Silicon (M4 16GB is a strong dev machine and will hide problems on weaker targets):
- Draw calls are the main limit. Targets reported: about 100 (maintainer quote, mobile), about 100-150 for mid-range 60 fps, and several hundred to low thousands on desktop. A city needs instanced buildings, props, cars, lamps and pedestrians; EverRealm gets hundreds of houses down to a handful of calls with one InstancedMesh per model per chunk.
- Triangles: the sources say 'a couple million' is fine on mid-range hardware. Only the draw-call figures come from a maintainer quote; the triangle figure is a blogger's estimate.
- Resolution and post-processing are the next costs. Cap devicePixelRatio and use a resolution slider or dynamic resolution. Each EffectComposer pass is a full-screen render, so rain, bloom and neon glow must be budgeted to one or two passes. The Vilnius prototype uses dynamic resolution and a frame-time governor.
- Lights: I found no cited source with a measured count of dynamic lights or shadows for browser games. Do not invent a number; the general practice implied by the sources is a few real lights plus emissive or baked neon and instanced decals. This is an open item to measure in a spike.
- Memory: Unity web is capped at a 2 GB heap, and iOS Safari crashes are reported. For Three.js the main leaks come from missing dispose() and large textures (resize to 2048 or less, use Draco/Meshopt). I found no authoritative per-tab texture memory limit number.
- Quality governor: both EverRealm and Vilnius ship adaptive quality, and EverRealm's is a one-way step-down to avoid oscillation. Plan for this from day one.
- WebGPU may reduce CPU overhead for draw-call-heavy scenes but is not guaranteed faster, so use the WebGL 2 fallback as the baseline and benchmark both.
research.load_time_and_size_notes: Hard numbers I verified: Godot 4.7.2 web export wasm 39.5 MB raw and about 10.1 MB gzip, engine only. Unity web heap max 2 GB. Three.js itself is a library of a few hundred KB, but I did not open a source stating the exact minified or gzipped size, so no figure is given. I found no published download size or load time for the Vilnius prototype (it streams from a server) or EverRealm. The 'Unity 230MB to 3.7MB' Reddit title is an unverified headline. For this game, model weight will dominate: city kits, cars and characters supplied as GLB/FBX should be converted to compressed GLB (Draco or Meshopt, KTX2 textures, 2048px max) and streamed by chunk behind a loading screen. Host limits matter: Cloudflare Pages 25 MiB per file, itch.io 200 MB per file / 500 MB total (as of Nov 2026 per the Ziva blog).
research.agent_workflow_notes: An AI agent can do most of this end-to-end in text: Vite plus Three.js, glTF pipeline scripts, Blender 5.3 headless for conversion and baking, and Playwright/headless Chromium for testing. The Vilnius repo is a concrete example: one script plays the game with key presses and checks physics, memory, frame times and console errors, and saves screenshots. Reported good practice: give the agent a browser and visual references, add in-game debug sliders (configurator), and use renderer.info (calls, triangles, geometries, textures) as an objective regression metric. Weak spots: headless Chromium uses software or limited GPU rendering, so fps numbers from CI are not representative of a real Safari or integrated GPU; the creator must play-test in real browsers. Feel (driving, camera, scoring), art direction and 'does it look good' still need a human or a reviewer model looking at screenshots. Evidence of agent-written code that was never verified is visible in the Vilnius repo (the uncompiled Unreal project). Unity is the weakest fit for this workflow here because the editor-centric scene and asset workflow is hard to drive from a terminal, and Unity is not installed; Godot has a text-based scene format and CLI export but a 39.5 MB engine wasm and no C# web export. I did not verify Unity's agent tooling.
strengths_for_this_game: Plain Three.js plus Vite is text-only and fully agent-drivable, with working open precedents (Vilnius driving prototype, EverRealm first-person open world) built by AI agents or solo developers
WebGPU is now shipped in Chrome/Edge 113+, Safari 26 (macOS and iOS), and Firefox on Windows and Apple Silicon Macs, and Three.js falls back to WebGL 2 automatically, so desktop coverage is wide
Instancing, chunk streaming, billboard-to-skinned crowd LOD and an adaptive quality governor are documented, working patterns that suit traffic and pedestrians
Headless Chromium automated play-testing with frame-time and memory checks is demonstrated in an actual repo
A night, rainy scene hides draw distance with fog and darkness, which suits chunk streaming (EverRealm uses fog to hide chunk edges)
risks_for_this_game: No verified precedent of a complete browser first-person driving game with traffic, police AI, scripted incidents and mission/menus; the closest examples are early prototypes or showcases without published sizes
Draw-call and CPU limits: a dense neon city with traffic and pedestrians needs disciplined instancing and merging; supplied unoptimised GLB/FBX assets are the most likely cause of failure
AI-built scenes typically skip dispose() and instancing, so budget a dedicated optimisation pass and use renderer.info as a metric
Rain, bloom and many dynamic lights are fill-rate and post-processing heavy; I found no measured light or shadow counts, so this needs an early spike on a real integrated GPU
Safari on desktop is shown as only 'partial' WebGPU support (macOS 26 and later), Firefox Android and Linux are partial, and WebGPU is not always faster, so the WebGL 2 path must be tested everywhere

Unity web: 2 GB heap, reported iOS Safari crashes, and an editor-heavy workflow that is poor for terminal agents; Godot web: 39.5 MB engine wasm, no C# web export, and threaded builds need special HTTP headers
Phones and tablets are a poor target: mobile draw-call budgets are about 100 and iOS memory crashes are reported
Three.js release churn (APIs removed in r186/r187) means pinning a version
M4 16GB results will overstate performance for typical integrated-GPU Windows laptops; test on weaker hardware
